Summary:

Cheng et al. present the molecular architecture of the active form of the human apoptosome, based on a number of focused cryo-EM reconstructions that were determined from a single dataset. Using this structure, the authors describe the putative interactions that drive oligomerization of Apaf-1, the interaction cytochrome c with the sensor domain, and the spiraling CARD disk at the center of the apoptosome, which interestingly involves association of only 4 of the 7 CARDs. This new structure is coupled with prior apoptosome structures, as well as with native gradient gels to present a model for oligomerization, wherein cytochrome c binding induces conformational rearrangements that allow for nucleotide exchange and apoptosome assembly. The work of the authors significantly extends beyond their prior contributions to the analysis of the intricacies of apoptosome formation, and their model also provides novel insight into how caspase-9 may be activated on this signalling platform. The work also complements recent structural studies published by their international peers. One of the most striking findings of the authors is that their structural information might explain the current contradiction of how a supposedly heptavalent platform for caspase-9 activation is providing only a low number of active caspase-9 sites.

Overall the cryoEM analysis is well-done, and the authors show great expertise in their treatment of the data, using focused classification and other advanced image processing techniques to improve the resolution of disordered or flexible regions of the apoptosome complex. The overall quality of the density is consistent with the interpretation presented in the manuscript.

Essential revisions:

1) The "global" resolution is stated to be at 4.1 Angstroms resolution, yet a soft 3D mask was applied for this estimation – was this mask generated automatically, or manually, and more importantly, did this mask include the disordered sensor domains or CARD disk? If any structural features were cropped through the masking, then the reported "global" resolution is misleading.

2) The Resmap software is widely used by the EM community estimate local resolutions due to its ease of use. However, this software has repeatedly been shown to over-estimate resolutions. Comparison of the Resmap output with a similar program available in the Bsoft package is encouraged to ensure that the resolution claims are seen to be credible with map quality.

3) The PDB map associated with the combined EM density was generated by rigid body fitting previously determined crystal structures into the density, and these atomic models were refined into the density using a combination of MDFF and Phenix. For regions where side-chain densities are not clearly visible, the authors should limit the deposition to a C-α trace of the backbone.

4) Previous studies have shown that caspase-9 dimer activities towards procaspase-3 differ substantially from caspase-9 activities on apoptosomes. Can the structural model explain this phenomenon? In particular, can an allosteric contribution by the apoptosome backbone be excluded or substantiated? The authors also briefly touch on and somehow exclude the anti-dogmatic idea that caspase-9 monomers may be activated on the apoptosome backbone. It is not clear to me why that idea is or can be refuted. Would it be possible that both homodimers of active casp-9 can be formed on the apoptosome as well as active monomers? The authors should also explain better whether their structural model is consistent with the finding that the apoptosome can act as a molecular timer. Other than that, data presented in Figure 6D would probably be more convincing if the authors added a repeat in which a binding deficient PC9 was used as a negative control. Another suggestion is to comment on whether the data on cyt-c integration into the apoptosome and the contact regions (subsection “Sensor β-propellers and cytochrome c binding”, fourth paragraph) corresponds to cyt-c residues found to be critical for its proapoptotic potential (see e.g. published studies that compared yeast and human cyt-c).

5) The authors' structure of the platform of the pc-9 bound apoptosome and the unbound apoptosome recently reported by Zhou et al. 2015 is nearly identical (with the exception of the nucleotide orientation and whether Mg++ ions are involved in nucleotide binding), and for the most part the conclusions on the roles of cytochrome c and nucleotide binding in the formation of the apoptosome corroborate the findings of Zhou et.al. (2015). Perhaps more interesting is the increased resolution (~5.8 Angstroms) of the APAF-1:caspase-9 CARD disk and the confirmation of a previously postulated interaction of at least one catalytic caspase-9 P20/P10 dimer bound to the NBD ring of the central hub (Yuan et al. 2011). Previously, Akey's model of the apoptosome and caspase-9 (mostly from Yuan et al. 2010 and 2013) described the CARDs to be arranged in an acentric disk above the hub of a seven-spoked wheel of the apoptosome platform. The improved resolution of the disk reveals that it consists of 4 APAF-1 CARDS and 3 to 4 caspase-9 CARDS. Also, although their zipper like packing of APAF-1 and caspase-9 CARD domains differs from the crystal structure of the artificially created CARD disk of Hu et al. 2014, the author's structure is consistent with the existence of a second interface between the CARDs (dubbed type II interface) reported in that work. With one caspase-9 catalytic domain bound to the hub, this leaves the other two catalytic domains flexibly bound, potentially as an active dimer, though there is no evidence to verify this since the dimer is not resolved. The authors conclude that their model is consistent with the idea that the hub merely provides a platform for increasing the effective concentration of caspase-9 which drives dimerization and activation and that the caspase-9 catalytic domain is "parked" on the hub. However, their data in no way precludes that an as yet not understood allosteric mechanism accounts for the increased activity of apoptosome bound caspase-9. Indeed, Hu et al. 2015 identified mutations in APAF-1, K58E/K62E which are not found in any of the CARD:CARD interfaces and do not disturb apoptosome formation or recruitment of caspase-9, but severely interfere with the activity of the bound caspase-9. This suggests an allosteric mechanism exists for increased activation of apoptosome bound caspase-9. The author's only comment is that these mutations may affect binding of the CARD disc to the NBD hub. It would be helpful if they could elaborate on that further.

Other specific points:

In the first paragraph of the subsection “Domain and subunit interactions” – a list of residues potentially involved in lateral interactions in the central hub are listed. Are these based solely on the EM density? If so, the density should be included in a figure. Has mutagenesis been performed on these residues, or is there evidence of co-evolutionary variance to support these claims?

In the last paragraph of the subsection “Domain and subunit interactions” – some of the distances shown in Figure 3G & H are almost 5 Angstroms, which is beyond the range of hydrogen bonding. Due to the limited resolution of this region, it's possible that the modeling is inaccurate, so again, is there any other biochemical evidence supporting the role of the listed residues in stabilizing this region?

In the last paragraph of the subsection “Domain and subunit interactions” – The density described for the pi-cation interaction is questionable, if the authors want to include this statement, the density for this region should be shown in a figure.

In the third paragraph of the subsection “Sensor β-propellers and cytochrome c binding” – The authors state that all α-helices in cytochrome c are resolved. While the subunit can be unambiguously docked into the density, sausage-like densities that are consistent with α helices resolved to 6 Å resolution are not present.

In the fourth paragraph of the subsection “Sensor β-propellers and cytochrome c binding” – The interpretation of side-chain interactions based on docked crystal structures is appropriate, but discussion of visible Trp844 side chain density in a region where α helical densities are not discernible is over-interpretation.

In the third paragraph of the subsection “The CARD disk” – The authors mention that linker densities are visible, but the data is not shown. The symmetry mismatch in this region is a particularly interesting aspect of the manuscript, and the details of these linkers are relevant to understanding the mismatch – these linker densities should be shown. Despite their flexibility, is there any evidence of linker density for the linkers to the unassociated CARDs?

In the first paragraph of the subsection “A pc-9 catalytic domain on the hub” – Concerning the localization of the pc-9 catalytic domain – the authors' statement that EMAN2 uses a "density based approach in real space" needs further explanation. Is this simply cross-correlation-based projection matching? How is it different from other processing packages? The difference between the approach used in EMAN2 and RELION is not clear. Notably, a full description of the pc-9 processing is completely missing from the Methods section.

In the first paragraph of the subsection “A pc-9 catalytic domain on the hub” – Why is α-helical resolution reconstruction not shown? Do the p20 and p10 domains dock in with great accuracy into this reconstruction?

In the last paragraph of the subsection “A pc-9 catalytic domain on the hub” – How was alignment of composite map into the C1-symmetric pc-9-containing reconstruction performed? Is the cross correlation of this docked register substantially better than if it is docked into neighboring registers? Due to the speculative nature of this section, it's unclear what this paragraph adds to the manuscript.

results.result: The authors determined a near-atomic structure of the active human apoptosome by cryo-EM at 4.1 Å global resolution, with the central hub at 3-4 Å and peripheral regions at 4.5-10 Å resolution.
results.evaluation: The resolution claims are well-supported by gold standard FSC curves (C17), ResMap analysis (C18-C19), and visibility of side chains in density maps. The use of focused 3D classification to improve local resolution for specific regions (C21) is methodologically sound and appropriately documented.

results.result: An acentric CARD disk sits atop the apoptosome platform, containing seven well-ordered CARDs (four Apaf-1 and three or four pc-9) arranged in a clockwise spiral, with the fourth pc-9 CARD at lower occupancy.
results.evaluation: The disk architecture is resolved at ~5.8 Å using focused 3D classification (C68). The spiral arrangement with specific positioning of Apaf-1 and pc-9 CARDs (C69-C72) is supported by clear density for CARD-NBD linkers (C74) and the acentric, tilted positioning (C77). The lower occupancy of the fourth pc-9 CARD (C70) is appropriately noted as a structural observation.

results.result: The central hub contains seven copies of NBD, HD1, and WHD in nested rings, with lateral interactions mediated by the ISM motif (α12-loop-α13) and extensive hydrogen bonding networks, and dATP bound at the NBD-HD1 interface.
results.evaluation: The structural claims are well-supported by the 3-4 Å resolution in the central hub region (C18), with clear visualization of α-helices, side chains, and interaction networks shown in Figure 3. The identification of specific residues involved in interactions (C28-C29) and nucleotide binding (C30) is appropriate for this resolution.

results.result: Cytochrome c binds between the 7- and 8-blade β-propellers in the V-shaped sensor domain, with preferential interaction with the 8-blade β-propeller through extensive van der Waals contacts involving seven lysine residues, inducing conformational changes in the β-propellers.
results.evaluation: The cytochrome c binding mode is supported by focused 3D classification achieving ~6.1 Å resolution for the sensor domain (C21). The correction of a ~90° rotation error from a previous model (C37) demonstrates improved accuracy. The identification of contact regions (C38-C40) and specific lysine residues (C41) is reasonable at this resolution, though the authors appropriately note that higher resolution is needed for precise interaction details.

results.result: dATP binds in a pocket at the NBD-HD1 interface with the adenine base in an anti configuration in a hydrophobic pocket, and Ser325 acts as a modulator that may confer higher affinity for dATP over ATP by its proximity to the 2' carbon of the deoxyribose ring.
results.evaluation: The nucleotide binding site is well-resolved in the 3-4 Å central hub region. The anti configuration of the adenine base (C46, C48) is supported by comparison with other structures and re-fitting of the ground state structure. The proposed role of Ser325 as a modulator (C53-C54) is a reasonable inference based on structural proximity (~4 Å, C51) and comparison with Dark and CED-4, though functional validation would strengthen this claim.

results.result: The apoptosome has diverged from canonical AAA+ ATPases, lacking a stable Mg²⁺ binding site and arginine finger, which explains the very limited ATPase activity of Apaf-1 monomers (~4-5 ATP/hr) and no detectable activity in assembled apoptosomes.
results.evaluation: The absence of clear Mg²⁺ density (C57) and arginine finger (C56) is well-documented structurally. The comparison with CED-4 showing replacement of a key Mg²⁺ ligand (Lys191→Ser186) supports the structural basis for low activity. The cited ATPase measurements (C55, C65) provide functional validation. This represents a well-integrated structural-functional result.

results.result: Cytochrome c binding is a prerequisite for nucleotide exchange during apoptosome assembly, as demonstrated by native gel experiments showing that cytochrome c alone causes band shifts and aggregation, while dATP alone does not, but together they produce proper assembly.
results.evaluation: The native gel experiments (C60-C61, Figure 6A) provide direct biochemical evidence for the sequential binding model. The observation that cytochrome c causes aggregation in the absence of nucleotide exchange (C60) while dATP alone has no effect supports the proposed mechanism (C59). The structural basis for this sequence is explained by conformational changes that would make the nucleotide binding site more accessible.

results.result: pc-9 can form a 1:1 complex with Apaf-1 mediated by CARD-CARD interactions, and the cellular concentrations of pc-9 (~30 nM) and Apaf-1 (~340 nM) in HeLa cells suggest a ratio of approximately 1:10-11.
results.evaluation: The 1:1 complex formation is demonstrated by band shift experiments (C66, Figure 6D), including thrombin cleavage controls. The concentration estimates (C67) are appropriately cited from the literature. These results support the possibility of pre-formed Apaf-1/pc-9 heterodimers during assembly, though the authors appropriately note this is speculative.

results.result: The CARD disk architecture differs from previous models, with only four of seven Apaf-1 CARDs incorporated (three excluded and disordered), pc-9 CARDs located on the top surface without direct hub contacts, and Type I and II interfaces becoming progressively distorted around the spiral.
results.evaluation: The disk structure at ~5.8 Å resolution clearly shows only four Apaf-1 CARDs with visible linkers (C73-C74), supporting the exclusion of three CARDs (C75-C76). The positioning of pc-9 CARDs on the top surface (C79) and the distinction from the three-layer model (C80) are well-documented. The progressive distortion of interfaces (C82-C84) is a logical consequence of the spiral geometry and is supported by RMSD measurements.

results.result: Apaf-1 CARD mutations K58E and K62E that diminish pc-9 activation are located on the bottom surface of the disk and may interfere with CARD-NBD ring interactions rather than direct pc-9 binding.
results.evaluation: The structural localization of these mutations (C87) provides a plausible alternative explanation for their functional effects (C86), distinct from disrupting CARD-CARD interfaces. This demonstrates how the structure can reinterpret existing mutagenesis data, though the mechanism remains inferential without additional experiments.

results.result: Catalytic domains from a single pc-9 can be 'parked' on the central hub adjacent to the disk in approximately 50% of particles, with two possible positions near the pc-9 CARD at position 2p, suggesting one catalytic domain may be parked when an odd number of zymogens are bound.
results.evaluation: While density for parked catalytic domains is observed in c1 refinements (C88-C89), the authors acknowledge this feature could not be resolved with focused 3D classification in RELION and shows local heterogeneity. The 50% occupancy (C91) and two possible positions (C90) indicate significant uncertainty. The stoichiometry inference (C4-C6) relies on combining structural observations with literature measurements, making this result less definitive than the core structural findings.

results.result: The heptameric platform is mostly unchanged during pc-9 activation relative to the ground state, with an RMSD of 1.7 Å for Cα atoms when comparing Apaf-1 and cytochrome c.
results.evaluation: The comparison with the ground state structure (Zhou et al., 2015) is appropriate and the 1.7 Å RMSD (C23) indicates high structural similarity. This validates that the major difference between ground state and active apoptosomes is the presence of the CARD disk, supporting the functional model.

results.result: The structure suggests that 3-4 pc-9 molecules are tethered to the disk through CARD-CARD interactions, with parked catalytic domains held in reserve when odd numbers are bound, and remaining catalytic domains flexibly tethered, creating a dynamic proteolytic machine.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic model integrates structural observations with stoichiometry measurements from the literature (C93). However, the flexibility of catalytic domains (C97) means they are not directly visualized in most particles. The proposal that parked domains are held in reserve (C96) and the dynamic nature of the machine (C98) are reasonable inferences but remain speculative without additional functional or dynamic studies.

results.result: Active apoptosomes may contain either a 7-CARD disk with three pc-9 molecules and one flexibly-tethered dimer (plus one parked catalytic domain) or an 8-CARD disk with four pc-9 molecules and two flexibly-tethered dimers, with the 7-CARD configuration favored under the experimental conditions and possibly in vivo.
results.evaluation: The lower occupancy of the pc-9 CARD at position 8p (C101) supports that 7-CARD disks predominate in vitro. However, the proposed stoichiometries (C99-C100) and the speculation about in vivo preference (C102) are models based on structural snapshots. The authors appropriately acknowledge these are speculative scenarios that would require additional validation, particularly regarding the number and activity of pc-9 dimers.

results.result: The structure suggests most active apoptosomes contain one or possibly two pc-9 dimers responsible for proteolytic activity, with flexibly-tethered catalytic domains that are stabilized by high local concentration on the apoptosome and require appropriate CARD-p20 linker length for optimal activation.
results.evaluation: This synthesis integrates structural observations with functional data from the literature (C103-C105, C107, C109). The inference that flexibly-bound catalytic domains cannot affect disk stability (C106) is reasonable but not directly tested. The requirement for high local concentration (C110) is supported by linker cleavage experiments, but the precise number of active dimers (C111) and their configuration remains uncertain due to the flexibility and heterogeneity of catalytic domain positioning.
